The city kept its lost property in a former swimming pool. The deep end held bicycles; the shallow end, umbrellas. On rainy days people came down the tiled steps and pointed to a black umbrella among two hundred others. When asked what distinguished it, they almost always said, “It’s mine,” with a conviction that made Ada wish this were admissible evidence.

She had worked there for eleven years. She knew that people embroidered their names into hats they disliked and left no identifying marks on things they couldn’t bear to lose. She knew that a child could describe a missing glove with greater precision than a grown man could describe his briefcase. She knew that if someone began by saying the object wasn’t worth much, the conversation would take a while.

One Tuesday a bus driver brought in a paper bag containing a single pear and a house key. The pear had ripened past the point at which Ada could put it on the shelf, and the key had nothing to distinguish it except a dot of yellow nail polish.

“Did you see who left it?”

“If I’d seen who left it,” the driver said, “I’d have shouted.”

Ada gave him a receipt for one key. After he left, she ate the pear over the staff sink. It was the best pear she’d had all year, and she felt briefly, absurdly, like a thief.

That afternoon a woman called about a blue casserole dish. Ada found three. The woman said hers had a chip on the handle, which eliminated one. Then she said there might be a little baked cheese stuck to the underside of the lid.

“There is,” Ada said.

“Oh, good. My sister said she soaked it.”

The woman came in the next morning and carried the dish away wrapped in a bath towel. She was six steps up when she turned around.

“Did you have to look at the cheese?”

“Yes.”

“Sorry about that.”

“It was a very small amount of cheese,” Ada said, and the woman went on up.

At home Ada had a drawer full of keys to places she no longer lived. One opened a flat above a bakery where she had learned to sleep through the arrival of flour. Another belonged to a building that had been demolished. She could have thrown that one out, but she liked the definiteness of it. There was no risk of discovering she still needed it.

The yellow-dotted key remained on the shelf for two weeks. Then a boy came in for a trumpet and, while Ada was checking the serial number, asked whether anybody ever left food on the bus.

“All the time,” she said. “Why?”

“Just wondered.”

He was wearing a school uniform with the knees gone shiny. His mother stood at the counter, buying time for him to check that everything was in the case. He counted the mouthpieces twice. There was only one.

“What kind of food?” Ada asked.

“A pear, maybe.”

His mother looked at him. “You said you ate that.”

“I was going to.”

Ada took the key down from the shelf. The mother put her hand flat on the counter.

“I changed the lock,” she said.

“Good,” said the boy. He closed the trumpet case and opened it again.

“I thought you’d dropped it outside the house.”

“I thought so too.”

Ada set the receipt beside the key and turned it so the mother could read the date. The mother had paid a locksmith on a Sunday. She told Ada the price, then told her how long the man had been there, which was twenty minutes. She seemed to be hoping that Ada, who had a municipal badge and a pen on a chain, might be able to do something with these facts.

“Was the pear still in the bag?” the boy asked.

“Yes,” Ada said.

“Was it any good?”

“It was excellent.”

“I told you it was ripe,” his mother said. “You always wait until they’re brown.”

For a moment the boy looked as if he might object. Instead he put the old key in the little compartment beside the mouthpiece and snapped the case shut. His mother reached for the handle, but he was already carrying it.

That evening Ada went home by way of the bakery. It was still there, although the bread was displayed in the window now, where the sacks of flour used to go. The man behind the counter was slicing a loaf for a customer. Ada joined the queue. She hadn’t meant to buy anything, but once she was inside she remembered how good the bread was toasted.

When it was her turn, she asked who lived upstairs.

“I do,” the man said. “Why?”

She told him about the key. He wiped his hands on his apron and said he’d had some trouble with that lock. If she still had the key, would she mind bringing it in? The spare his landlord had given him didn’t work.

The next day she brought all the keys, having discovered she couldn’t tell the bakery key from the one to the demolished building. The man put a sign in the window and led her around the side. The first key wouldn’t go in. The second went in but wouldn’t turn. The third opened the door.

From the bottom of the stairs Ada could see the old green paint on the banister, worn through to the wood where she had put her hand every morning. There was also a pair of enormous orange slippers on the landing. She had been about to ask if she could go up and look. The slippers made her realize what an odd request that would be.

“Do you want to keep it?” the man asked.

“No,” she said, and gave him the key.

He lifted the door slightly by the handle as he locked it. She’d forgotten about that. In winter, when the wood swelled, she used to have to lift it with both hands.

“Does the bedroom still smell of bread in the morning?” she asked.

The man considered this. “I don’t notice it anymore.”

Neither had she, by the time she moved out. But she noticed it now, standing beside him in the narrow passage, and stayed until he had tested the key once more.
